You should try the following : check your connection, disable ad-blocker, clear your browser cache, try in private mode, try from another browser/computer/connection. 0 The Gnomes of Zavandor Welcome to the world of The Gnomes of Zavandor. Like most gnomes, you have two great passions: sparkling gems and wondrous machines. The sought-after gemstones can be found around the mining town of Diamantina. They can be bought and sold at the gem exchange, shady traders are always willing to engage in a little wheeling and dealing, and then you can use the gems to claim valuable mining rights, artifacts and jewellery. Who will become the most successful gem trading mogul? Zavandor is a fantasy setting which revolves around a capitalist economy based on trading in gems - sapphires, rubies, mystical gems etc. Other games in the family include Mines of Zavandor, and The Scepter of Zavandor. Gnomes of Zavandor features two central boards. The first is a grid with markers indicating the current price of each of the gem types, and also indicating whether the price is going to go up or down next turn. Gems can be bought (or sold) for cash in the first phase of each turn. Buying gems makes them more valuable in subsequent turns; selling them reduces their value, and this is reflected on the grid. These gems can be used to buy tiles from the second board, a star-shaped arena featuring 'mining rights' tiles positioned randomly around it. The position on the board indicates the cost to purchase these mining rights; the cost will be a mixed selection of coloured gems. At the end of each turn, players gain new gems according to the mining rights they have acquired and this affects the central economy, generally reducing the value of the relevant gems when they are purchased for hard cash, in future rounds. The initial phase of the turn involves buying gems, selling gems, taking gold, trading with the central supply, and purchasing cards and tokens (with gems rather than cash). The items available for purchase include equipment improving your efficiency, jewels providing victory points, and mining rights. The second phase of the turn involves mining for new gems. Each player takes the gems they are allowed according to their mining rights. At the end of each turn, the market values are adjusted according to the actions which have occurred; the price of the available equipment is discounted (this rule is optional); and another area of the star-shaped board becomes accessible with more mining-rights available to purchase in the next round. The game continues until one player has reached a victory-point target, dependent on the number of players in the game. Victory points are achieved by purchasing mining-rights, equipment, and most significantly (but also most expensively) jewellery. [Rating: 2/10] 2023-07-31 : First play. Ouch, what a letdown. Uninteresting and unbalanced mess of a game.

[Rating: 3/10] Hard to envision what sort of economy they were trying to model here, but it doesn't seem to work. The inflationary boost of purchasing an item or mining right doesn't seem ti have an adequate counterbalance and the prices quickly hit the roof leaving nothing to differentiate the gem types. Have a hard time imagining myself wanting to play this again.  First mines, now this - I guess Scepter really was a one off.

[Rating: 3/10] The Gnomes of Zavandor is [i]yet another[/i] "engine-building" resource conversion game, this time featuring gems, money, and actions as the resources you're converting into Victory Points. The whole "commodity speculation" component is pretty weak, as the gem values don't fluctuate that much. Mostly it's about getting the right combination of gems at the right time, so you can improve your "engine," which in turn gives you more gems/actions/money so you can do the same thing all over again. [Rating: 3/10] On the surface this seems like a game about strategically investing in mining rights and racing to craft the best jewelry; but in reality the artifacts make the game about stockpiling, waiting, and racing to buy the hoovermatic so you can laugh at the fools who wasted their gems on mining rights. Avoid!

[Rating: 3/10] Overly long for how little the game builds upon itself or anything. I like the player manipulated stock market aspect, but that isn't enough of a reason to come back to this game. Dry. Weird theme. Slightly worried about balance but not interested in returning to see if that is true or not.

[Rating: 4/10] Not a bad game, but not one that stands out as worthy of repeated play. Why on earth does Lookout insist on branding its games as if they were designed by Knizia? Who is invested in the Zavandor world?

[Rating: 4/10] Quite a weird game, this one.  Money is very tight, and you'll find it hard to buy the gems you need to trade for the VP cards, but this is good as it puts more emphasis on the mining tiles which seem to reward planning.  The 3 actions per round never seem like quite enough, and it can be quite agonising to work out what to do each round to maximise profits, but that's the point I suppose.  I don't much like the Artifacts (basically, player powers) that can be bought, but they add some flavour to proceedings. [Rating: 4/10] This game has one of the finest 'First Player Markers' ever devised by the mind of man. If you want a great FPM then this game is for you.
